summary: Taito is a Japanese arcade and video-game company whose coin-operated catalogue supplied many properties later converted for home computers. The CCG archive represents its Commodore publishing activity rather than the much larger arcade catalogue.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves home-computer software carrying the Taito publishing credit.
Taito arcade properties were frequently converted for 8-bit and 16-bit computers by external development and publishing partners.
note: Developer and territorial publishing credits can differ on Taito conversions, so individual CCG game records retain the credit attached to the represented version.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Taito games

summary: Taskset was an early British Commodore 64 developer and publisher whose catalogue concentrated on arcade-style original games during the machine's first commercial years.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Taskset Commodore 64 releases including Cosmic Convoy, Pipeline, Gyropod, Bozo's Night Out and Super Pipeline II.
Its preserved C64 catalogue credits programmers including Andy Walker, Paul Hodgson, Tony Gibson and Mark Harrison.
note: The surviving institutional catalogue is stronger than the corporate record, so this profile avoids unsupported claims about ownership or formation dates.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Taskset C64 games

summary: Team17 was formed in 1990 and established itself as one of the Amiga's defining independent developers and publishers. Its early catalogue included Full Contact, Alien Breed, Project-X and several externally developed releases before Worms broadened the company's reach.
facts: Team17's official history records the company being founded by Debbie Bestwick, Martyn Brown and Michael Robinson on 7 December 1990.
The company says its first game was Full Contact for the Commodore Amiga in 1991, followed by Alien Breed.
Team17's own archive describes its early strategy as developing and publishing games with a strong initial focus on the Amiga.
note: The profile concerns Team17's original Amiga-era activity represented by CCG rather than its much larger modern publishing catalogue.

sources.label: Team17 — official company history
Team17 — 1991-92 game archive

summary: Tengen was an Atari Games publishing label used for home versions of arcade properties during the late 1980s and early 1990s. Its appearance in the CCG archive reflects that home-software publishing role.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves software carrying the Tengen publishing credit across home-computer and console platforms.
Tengen releases were closely associated with home versions of arcade games originating from Atari Games and other licensed properties.
note: Tengen and Atari are kept distinct when the represented release carries the Tengen label.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Tengen games

summary: Terminal Software was an early British home-computer publisher with a substantial Commodore 64 presence. Its preserved catalogue includes arcade-style games, compilations and titles written both internally and by named individual programmers.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Terminal Software C64 releases including Hunter, Stellar Dodger, Super Dogfight, Super Gridder, Plumb Crazy and Triple Tournament.
The museum credits Reg Stevens on Super Gridder and R. W. Stevens on Super Dogfight, while several other releases simply carry Terminal or Terminal Software as author.
note: Company-level documentation is limited, so the profile stays with preserved publishing activity rather than speculative ownership history.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Terminal Software C64 games

summary: The Edge was a British home-computer publisher active through the 1980s, releasing original titles, arcade conversions and games from external development teams across the major 8-bit platforms.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Commodore 64 releases under The Edge publishing credit including Quo Vadis, Wizardry and Garfield: Winter's Tail.
The museum also records The Edge publishing titles such as Fairlight and Bobby Bearing on other British home-computer formats.
note: The Edge sometimes shared publishing credit with arcade rights holders such as Konami; CCG retains the credit attached to each represented release.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — The Edge C64 games

summary: The One Amiga appears in the CCG archive as a magazine-associated software publishing credit. Cover-disk and magazine software releases form a distinct part of the Amiga ecosystem and are retained separately from conventional commercial publishers.
facts: The CCG archive records an Amiga title carrying The One Amiga publishing credit.
Magazine-distributed software is kept as its own publisher route where that is the credit attached to the archived release.
note: This is intentionally a modest profile because The One's role here is magazine software distribution rather than a conventional standalone game publisher.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — The One magazine collection

summary: The Sales Curve was a British game publisher and production company active around the transition from 8-bit home computers to 16-bit systems and consoles. The CCG archive preserves its Commodore publishing credit separately from later company names.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves software carrying The Sales Curve publishing credit.
The company's historical catalogue spans arcade conversions and externally developed games across several home-computer formats.
note: Later corporate identities are not merged into this route because CCG follows the publisher name printed on the represented release.

summary: Thor Computer Software was a Liverpool-area publishing name linked to the operation that later used the Odin Computer Graphics identity for in-house game development.
facts: The Centre for Computing History's Odin company record states that Odin had previously published games under the Thor name.
The change to Odin Computer Graphics accompanied the decision to develop games in-house rather than continuing only as a publishing operation.
note: Thor and Odin remain separate archive routes because they are distinct historical publishing names on the represented software.

facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves software under the Tikkurila publishing credit.
No founder or corporate-history claims are added because the surviving game-publishing record is limited.
note: The intentionally narrow wording prevents this historical software credit being confused with unrelated modern businesses using the same name.

summary: Timeworks was a personal-computer software publisher whose catalogue extended beyond games into productivity and educational software. Its presence in the CCG archive reflects the Commodore software credit attached to the represented title.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves software carrying the Timeworks publishing credit across personal-computer platforms.
Timeworks published software for Commodore computers alongside non-game productivity products during the 1980s.
note: This archive page concerns the game/software release represented by CCG, not the publisher's broader productivity catalogue.

summary: Titus Software was a French developer and publisher whose computer-game catalogue expanded across 8-bit and 16-bit systems before moving heavily into consoles. Its Commodore releases form a small part of that wider catalogue.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves home-computer games carrying the Titus Software publishing credit.
The museum records Titus as both developer and publisher on releases including Off Shore Warrior, illustrating its dual production and publishing role.
note: The profile stays catalogue-focused because reliable institutional evidence is stronger for the software output than for a concise corporate timeline.

facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves home-computer software carrying the Tronix Publishing credit.
The label appears during the early commercial period of Commodore 64 game publishing.
note: Only documented publishing activity is presented because reliable company-history material is limited.

facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Commodore software carrying the TV Games publishing credit.
The surviving catalogue evidence is stronger than the company record, so no unsupported ownership or formation claims are included.

summary: Tynesoft was a prolific British home-computer publisher whose catalogue covered Acorn, Commodore, Sinclair, Amstrad and Atari systems. It released original games, sports titles and licensed properties throughout the 1980s.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves a large multi-platform Tynesoft catalogue covering numerous British home computers.
Its preserved Commodore releases include Super Gran, Roller Coaster Rumbler and Beverly Hills Cop alongside software for the C16 and Plus/4 family.
The archive shows Tynesoft working both as publisher and as credited developer on different releases.
note: The profile uses institutional catalogue evidence and does not add unsupported corporate-origin claims.

summary: Ubisoft was founded in France in 1986 by the five Guillemot brothers to create and distribute video games. Its earliest home-computer output included Zombi before the company expanded into a major international developer and publisher.
facts: Ubisoft's official history states that the five Guillemot brothers founded the company in 1986.
The company says it was created to develop and distribute video games around the world.
Ubisoft identifies Zombi as one of its first home-computer releases.
note: The CCG route uses the historical 'Ubi Soft' spelling recorded on the represented Amiga release while the company now styles its name Ubisoft.

sources.label: Ubisoft — official company story

summary: Ultimate Play The Game was the publishing name of Ashby Computers and Graphics Ltd, the British company formed by Tim and Chris Stamper. Its technically ambitious 8-bit games became highly influential on the ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64.
facts: The Centre for Computing History records Ultimate Play The Game as the publishing name of Ashby Computers and Graphics Ltd.
The museum states that brothers Tim and Chris Stamper formed the company in 1982 after working as arcade developers.
Ultimate's Commodore 64 catalogue included a group of Arthur Pendragon adventures beginning with The Staff of Karnath.
note: The profile concerns the historical Ultimate Play The Game publishing identity represented in the CCG archive.

facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves software carrying the VIFI International publishing credit.

summary: Virgin Mastertronic was created when Mastertronic's business was combined with Virgin Games during the late 1980s. The name spans the final years of the classic budget-software operation and the group's growing involvement in wider games and console distribution.
facts: The Mastertronic Collectors Archive records Virgin Group buying into Mastertronic in 1987 and the business later being merged with Virgin Games to create Virgin Mastertronic.
Former Mastertronic financial controller Anthony Guter records staff from Mastertronic and Virgin Games joining forces in London in 1988.
The Centre for Computing History preserves Virgin Mastertronic releases for Commodore, Sinclair and DOS systems.
note: Virgin Mastertronic remains a distinct route because the name appears directly on releases represented in the CCG archive.

summary: Windham Classics was a specialist interactive-fiction label associated with literary adaptations for home computers. Its presence in the CCG archive reflects that story-led publishing niche.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves home-computer software carrying the Windham Classics publishing credit.
The label's catalogue concentrated on narrative and literary adventure software rather than arcade-style games.
note: The profile remains catalogue-focused because reliable public corporate-history material for the label is limited.

summary: Zeppelin Games was a British budget and mid-price publisher active around the end of the 8-bit era and into the early 16-bit years. Its catalogue covered sports, action and arcade-style releases across several home-computer formats.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Zeppelin Games releases across Commodore, Sinclair, Atari and Amstrad systems.
Its recorded Commodore catalogue includes International Tennis, World Soccer, Jocky Wilson's Dart Challenge and Amiga releases such as Arnie and Arcade Fruit Machine.
The archive records Zeppelin acting both as publisher and, on some releases, as the credited development team.
note: The publisher later appears alongside other budget labels on compilation software; CCG keeps the Zeppelin credit attached to the represented releases.
